newsitem.title: UK: It's spend, spend, spend but Britons don't know it.
newsitem.headline: It's spend, spend, spend but Britons don't know it.

text.p: The British are spending more than they earn but won't admit it to themselves.

People who curbed their spending habits to get through the recession of the early 1990s now feel they need a "pat on the back" for enduring so many years of financial stringency, according to a report published on Tuesday.
Britons are buying themselves presents because they feel they need a reward for a bad day at the office, market research company Mintel said.

But instead of the ostentatious "big ticket" items on which they splashed out in the 1980s boom --- furniture and home extensions -- they are now buying themselves cheaper treats like magazines, chocolates, takeaway meals and visits to the cinema.
Mintel said consumer spending had risen by 10.5 percent over the past five years while disposable income went up by 8.8 percent.
But because people are adopting a "drip feed" approach to spending on their treats, they do not realise how much it actually amounts to, it said.
"We are spending more than our incomes -- it's hidden away in the figures -- but we don't realise that," said Mintel's statistician Peter Ayton.
Part is fuelled by credit and part by people running down some of the savings they put away during the last recession.

Another area where the "indulgence factor" comes into play is women's clothes, Ayton said. One woman Mintel had spoken to said she bought new dresses as "an act of rebellion against the injustice of it all".
She added: "I know I can't afford it but I still go out and do it anyway."

Mintel said the concept of the treat as a means of cheering oneself up was better understood by women than by men, possibly because men felt that everything they bought for themselves was a necessity which they did not have to justify.
More money is also being spent on gambling, Mintel said, with betting losses as a proportion of expenditure having increased nearly threefold over the past decade.
The National Lottery, introduced in November 1995, is playing its part in boosting gambling losses.
The survey showed that couples were starting families later and women were also tending to return to work after having children more than in the past.
This meant the domestic service market had quadrupled over the past 10 years and was now worth four billion pounds ($6.5 billion).

But as social trends shift, old worries will not go away, Mintel said. Among the working population of 20 to 54-year-olds, 40 percent said they worried about not having enough money to live and 56 percent were concerned about health. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
